title: Design a Chat App (WhatsApp)
summary: End-to-end walkthrough of a WhatsApp-style chat: WebSocket gateways, cross-server routing, per-conversation ordering, offline sync, receipts, presence and media.
body:
## Practice first

Design a mobile-first chat app in the style of WhatsApp: people chat one-to-one and in groups, messages arrive instantly when the recipient is online and are waiting for them when they come back, senders see "delivered" and "read" ticks, and one account can be used on a phone and a laptop at the same time.

Spend about 10 minutes sketching before reading on: requirements, entities, the client-server protocol, a baseline that delivers a message between two phones on different servers, and the deep dives you would pick. Then compare. This is one defensible design, not the only one.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Send messages** in one-to-one chats and in groups of up to 500 members, and see them in real time when online.
2. **Receive messages sent while offline** as soon as they reconnect, on every device logged in to their account, in the same order everyone else sees.
3. **See delivery and read status** for messages they sent.

Stretch, covered in deep dives: **media** (photos, video, voice notes) and **presence** ("online", "last seen").

Out of scope: voice and video calls, stories, payments, message search, and the cryptography of end-to-end encryption. We do note its consequence: with end-to-end encryption the server stores and routes ciphertext and cannot read, rank or search message content.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** 500M daily active users, about 200M connected at peak, sending ~20 billion messages per day.
- **Latency:** p99 under 500 ms from send to display when both parties are online in the same region.
- **Ordering:** per-conversation total order; every member and device sees a conversation's messages in the same order. No global order across conversations is needed.
- **Durability:** once the sender's client shows the single tick (server acknowledgement), the message must never be lost. Delivery is at-least-once; clients dedupe.
- **Availability vs consistency, per feature:** message send and history favour consistency of order within a conversation; presence and typing indicators favour availability and may be stale or dropped.

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **Message rate:** 20B / 86,400 s ≈ 230,000 messages/s average; peaks around 3x, ~700k/s. Too many writes for one database: the message store must be **partitioned**, and a write-optimised wide-column store (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable style) fits an append-heavy, read-by-range workload.
- **Deliveries, not messages, dominate:** if 20% of messages go to groups averaging 20 members, deliveries per second ≈ 230k × (0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 20) ≈ 1.1M/s. Fan-out cost scales with group size, which is why large groups get their own path.
- **Connections:** 200M concurrent sockets at ~50k per gateway host (memory per connection plus TLS) ≈ 4,000 gateways. A message's sender and recipient are almost always on different hosts, so we need **explicit routing**; broadcasting every message to 4,000 hosts is out.
- **Storage:** ~100 bytes of payload plus ~100 bytes of metadata ≈ 200 B × 20B ≈ 4 TB/day before replication. Retention policy is a real decision: keeping full history forever means petabytes per year; keeping undelivered messages only (the original WhatsApp approach) is far cheaper but makes new-device history sync harder. We keep history with a configurable retention and time-bucketed partitions.

## Core entities

- **User** and **Device**: a user has several devices; each device has its own connection, push token and sync cursor.
- **Conversation**: id, type (direct or group), metadata. **Membership**: conversation, user, role, joined-at.
- **Message**: conversation id, per-conversation sequence number, client message id, sender, body (ciphertext), optional media reference, server timestamp.
- **Receipt watermark**: per conversation and member, `delivered_up_to_seq` and `read_up_to_seq`.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USER ||--o{ DEVICE : uses
    USER ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP : has
    CONVERSATION ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP : includes
    CONVERSATION ||--o{ MESSAGE : contains
    MEMBERSHIP ||--|| RECEIPT_WATERMARK : tracks
```

Storing receipts as watermarks rather than one row per message per reader is a key simplification: "read up to 1042" covers every earlier message, so a 500-member group generates one small update per reader instead of 500 rows per message.

## API

Real-time traffic uses one WebSocket per device (TLS, authenticated with a device token at connect). Frames are small JSON or protobuf messages:

```text
client -> server  { "type": "send", "clientMsgId": "c-8f1", "conversationId": "cv_9",
                    "body": "<ciphertext>", "mediaId": null }
server -> client  { "type": "ack", "clientMsgId": "c-8f1", "seq": 1043, "ts": 1761700000 }
server -> client  { "type": "message", "conversationId": "cv_9", "seq": 1043,
                    "senderId": "u_1", "body": "<ciphertext>" }
client -> server  { "type": "receipt", "conversationId": "cv_9",
                    "kind": "read", "upToSeq": 1043 }
client -> server  { "type": "sync", "cursor": "inbox:88120" }
```

Request/response operations use HTTPS:

```text
POST /v1/conversations                     { "type": "group", "memberIds": [...] }
POST /v1/conversations/{id}/members        { "userId": "u_7" }
GET  /v1/conversations/{id}/messages?beforeSeq=1000&limit=50   (history paging)
POST /v1/media                             -> { "mediaId", "uploadUrl" }  (presigned)
```

`clientMsgId` is generated on the device and makes resends idempotent. History pages by sequence number, never by offset.

## High-level design

**Send and receive in real time.** Devices connect through a layer-4 load balancer to **chat gateways**, which hold sockets and little logic. A gateway forwards a `send` frame to the **message service**, which checks membership, assigns the next sequence number for the conversation, writes the message to the **message store**, acknowledges the sender, and looks up where each recipient device is connected in the **connection registry** (`device_id → gateway_id`, kept in Redis with heartbeat-refreshed TTLs). It publishes the message to each target gateway's channel, and the gateway pushes it down the socket.

**Receive while offline, on every device.** If a recipient device has no live connection, the message is already durable in the store; the service also appends a pointer to the user's **inbox** and asks the **push service** to wake the phone via APNs/FCM. On reconnect, each device syncs from its own cursor.

**Delivery and read status.** Recipient devices send `receipt` frames; the service advances the member's watermark and routes a receipt event back to the sender's devices the same way it routes messages.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C1["Sender device"] --> LB["L4 load balancer"]
    LB --> G1["Chat gateway 1"]
    G1 --> MS["Message service"]
    MS --> DB[("Message store")]
    MS --> IB[("Inbox index")]
    MS --> REG[("Connection registry")]
    MS --> PS[["Pub/sub per gateway"]]
    PS --> G2["Chat gateway 2"]
    G2 --> C2["Recipient device"]
    MS --> PUSH["Push service"]
    PUSH --> APN["APNs and FCM"]
    C1 --> MEDIA["Media service"]
    MEDIA --> BLOB[("Blob storage and CDN")]
```

Walk one message through it. Alice's phone (gateway 1) sends "hi" to Bob. The message service assigns seq 1043 in conversation `cv_9`, writes it with a quorum write, appends `(cv_9, 1043)` to Bob's inbox, and acks Alice: one tick. The registry says Bob's phone is on gateway 2 and his laptop is offline. The service publishes to gateway 2's channel; gateway 2 pushes the frame; Bob's phone sends `delivered up to 1043`, which is routed back to Alice: two ticks. Bob's laptop gets nothing now, but will sync from its cursor when it opens, and a push notification is sent if no device of Bob's is online.

## Deep dives

### 1. Routing a message to the right gateway (latency at 4,000 servers)

**Problem:** the recipient's socket lives on one of thousands of gateways, devices move between gateways on every reconnect, and groups multiply the work.

- **Bad: broadcast to every gateway.** Each gateway receives every message and discards 99.97% of them. At 1M deliveries/s that is billions of wasted operations per second.
- **Good: a pub/sub channel per user.** On connect, the gateway subscribes to `user:{id}`; the message service publishes to the recipient's channel without knowing where they are. Simple, but Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget, and millions of subscribe/unsubscribe operations churn as phones reconnect.
- **Great: connection registry plus per-gateway channels, with a separate path for big groups.** The registry maps each device to its gateway; the service batches all recipients on the same gateway into one publish to `gateway:{id}` (or a direct gRPC stream). For groups above a threshold (say 100 members), the service writes once and hands fan-out to **delivery workers** reading a Kafka topic partitioned by conversation, so a 500-member group does not block the sender's ack.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Alice phone
    participant G1 as Gateway 1
    participant M as Message service
    participant S as Message store
    participant R as Registry
    participant G2 as Gateway 2
    participant B as Bob phone
    A->>G1: send clientMsgId c-8f1
    G1->>M: forward
    M->>S: write cv_9 seq 1043
    M-->>G1: ack seq 1043
    G1-->>A: single tick
    M->>R: where are Bob's devices
    R-->>M: phone on gateway 2
    M->>G2: publish to gateway 2
    G2->>B: message seq 1043
    B->>G2: delivered up to 1043
```

The order is the important part: persist first, ack the sender, then deliver. Pub/sub is the fast path, the store is the source of truth; if the publish is lost (a gateway restart, a dropped Redis message), the recipient recovers it through sync in deep dive 3. A stale registry entry costs one wasted publish; the gateway replies "not here", and the service treats the device as offline.

Gateways themselves need care: long-lived connections make deploys disruptive, so drain gradually (stop accepting, tell clients to reconnect with jittered backoff over several minutes) to avoid a reconnect storm.

### 2. Ordering and duplicates within a conversation (ordering requirement)

**Problem:** two members of a group send at the same moment from different gateways; mobile clients retry sends on flaky networks. Everyone must see one order, and a retried send must not appear twice.

- **Bad: order by client timestamp.** Phone clocks are wrong by seconds or minutes; two devices disagree on order.
- **Good: server timestamp from the message service.** Better, but different service hosts have skewed clocks too, and ties are common at high rates.
- **Great: a per-conversation sequence number assigned by a single owner.** Route all writes for a conversation to one owner (hash `conversation_id` to a partition; the partition leader assigns `seq = last + 1` and writes it), or use an atomic counter per conversation (`INCR conv:{id}:seq`) before the write. Sequence numbers give a total order per conversation, gap detection (a device that has 1041 and receives 1043 knows to fetch 1042), and a natural paging key. The owner also keeps a short-lived map of `(sender, clientMsgId) → seq`, so a retried send returns the original ack instead of creating a new message.

A single owner per conversation is a throughput ceiling, but a chat with even a few hundred messages per second is extreme; the partitioned design scales with the number of conversations, not the size of any one. If the counter is a separate system from the store, a crash between `INCR` and the write leaves a gap; clients must tolerate gaps by asking for the range and accepting "no message at 1042".

Store messages partitioned by `(conversation_id, time_bucket)` and clustered by `seq` descending, so "latest 50 messages" and "messages after 1040" are single-partition range reads. The time bucket keeps very active conversations from creating unbounded partitions.

### 3. Offline delivery and multi-device sync (durability)

**Problem:** a phone goes into a tunnel for 20 minutes; a laptop was closed for a week; a new tablet logs in. Each must converge to exactly the messages it is missing, without the server tracking per-device delivery for every message.

- **Bad: per-device undelivered queue that the server deletes on delivery.** Works for one device, but with several devices the server stores one copy per device and must know which devices exist forever.
- **Good: each device asks every conversation "anything after seq N?"** Correct, but a user in 300 conversations would issue 300 queries on every reconnect.
- **Great: a per-user inbox index plus per-device cursors.** Every message appends a tiny entry `(inbox_seq, conversation_id, message_seq)` to each recipient's inbox, ordered by a per-user sequence. Each device stores the last inbox position it has processed. On reconnect it sends one `sync` with that cursor and gets back every pointer since, then fetches message bodies by conversation range. Inbox entries older than the retention window are trimmed; a device whose cursor is too old does a full resync of recent conversations.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as Bob laptop
    participant G as Gateway
    participant R as Registry
    participant M as Message service
    participant I as Inbox index
    participant S as Message store
    L->>G: connect, sync cursor 88120
    G->>R: register laptop on this gateway
    G->>M: sync after 88120
    M->>I: entries after 88120
    I-->>M: cv_9 up to 1043, cv_4 up to 77
    M->>S: fetch missing ranges
    S-->>M: message bodies
    M-->>G: batch, new cursor 88154
    G-->>L: deliver batch
    L->>G: ack cursor 88154
```

The laptop registers itself first, so live messages start flowing to it while it catches up; the sync and the live stream can overlap, and the client dedupes by `(conversation_id, seq)`. The cursor only advances after the client acknowledges, so a crash mid-sync just repeats the batch. Push notifications are a wake-up hint, not the delivery mechanism: APNs and FCM may coalesce or drop them, and the app always syncs from its cursor when it opens.

With end-to-end encryption each device has its own keys, so in practice the sender encrypts a copy per recipient device. That multiplies fan-out by devices per user and is why multi-device support was a large engineering project for encrypted messengers.

### 4. Receipts and presence (cheap, lossy, eventually consistent)

**Receipts:** devices send watermarks (`delivered up to`, `read up to`) and the service updates the membership row only if the new value is higher, so out-of-order or duplicate receipts are harmless. In a group, the sender's "read by everyone" is the minimum of members' read watermarks; compute it lazily when the sender opens message info instead of on every receipt. Batch receipts on the client (one per conversation per second) to cut traffic.

**Presence:** each connected device heartbeats every ~30 s, refreshing `presence:{user}` with a TTL of ~60 s; expiry means offline and sets `last_seen`. The expensive part is distribution: pushing every status change to everyone who has the user in their contacts is a fan-out storm. Instead, clients subscribe to presence only for the conversations on screen and the server pushes changes for those, falling back to fetching on demand. Presence is best-effort by design; users accept a "last seen" that is a minute off, and privacy settings may hide it entirely.

### 5. Media without clogging the chat path

Photos and videos never travel through the WebSocket. The client asks the media service for an upload slot and gets a **presigned URL** to blob storage, uploads directly (resumable or multipart for large videos), then sends a normal chat message whose body includes the media id, size, a content hash and a small inline thumbnail. Recipients download from a CDN using a short-lived signed URL. With end-to-end encryption the client encrypts the file with a random key and puts that key inside the encrypted message, so the blob store holds only ciphertext; forwarding the same file can reuse the blob by hash. Media gets its own retention and lifecycle policy, because it is most of the storage bill.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** WebSockets with a gateway tier, persist-before-deliver, a message table keyed by conversation, push notifications for offline users and a clear protocol with client message ids.
- **Senior:** explains cross-gateway routing with a registry or pub/sub, per-conversation sequence numbers instead of timestamps, reconnect sync from a cursor, receipts as watermarks, and why large groups need asynchronous fan-out. Quantifies connections and deliveries per second.
- **Staff:** reasons about operational and product edges: gateway deploys and reconnect storms, cross-region users, the cost of history retention, how end-to-end encryption multiplies fan-out and constrains server features, and which features are allowed to be lossy.

## Common mistakes

- Ordering by client or server wall-clock time.
- Delivering through pub/sub without persisting first, so a dropped publish loses the message.
- Treating push notifications as the delivery channel instead of a wake-up hint.
- Per-message, per-reader receipt rows in large groups.
- Sending media bytes over the chat socket.
- A design that works for one device per user and breaks when the same account opens on a laptop.
- Broadcasting presence changes to all contacts in real time.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] Gateways hold connections; a separate service validates, sequences and persists.
- [ ] The sender is acked only after a durable write; delivery is at-least-once with client dedupe on `(conversation, seq)`.
- [ ] Each conversation has a single sequence owner, and retries are idempotent via `clientMsgId`.
- [ ] A registry or channel scheme routes to the right gateway without broadcasting.
- [ ] Devices sync from their own cursor after reconnect; push is only a wake-up.
- [ ] Receipts are monotonic watermarks; presence uses heartbeats with TTLs and on-screen subscriptions.
- [ ] Large groups fan out asynchronously; media goes through presigned uploads and a CDN.

## Further reading

- [RFC 6455: The WebSocket Protocol](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6455)
- [Redis documentation: Pub/Sub](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/interact/pubsub/)
- [Discord engineering: How Discord stores billions of messages](https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-stores-billions-of-messages)
keyTakeaways: Separate connection gateways from the message service and route between them with a registry or per-gateway pub/sub channels.
Persist and ack before delivering; pub/sub is the fast path and the message store is the source of truth.
A per-conversation sequence number from a single owner gives total order, gap detection and idempotent retries.
A per-user inbox plus per-device cursors makes reconnects and multi-device sync one query; push is only a wake-up hint.
Receipts are monotonic watermarks, presence is lossy heartbeat state, and media goes around the socket through blob storage.
